Ford pulled the plug on the Escape last year after a 25-year run, but the crossover SUV could return as an EV on the new UEV platform.
Is Ford launching the Escape EV?
While Ford is preparing to launch the Fathom, its first vehicle based on the Universal Electric Vehicle (UEV) platform in 2027, the company is already hinting at what could be its second UEV-based model.
The last gas-powered Escape models rolled off the production line at Ford’s Louisville Assembly Plant as it retooled the facility to prepare for the new Fathom electric pickup.
Typically, when Ford retires a model, its landing page says something like “we’re discontinuing” it, or “it’s the end of the road,” such as with the Edge SUV.
Advertisement - scroll for more content
Meanwhile, the Escape landing page says the “SUV may be taking a breather for now,” declaring the “Ford Escape is tapping the brakes,” with no mention of it being discontinued. Instead, the site directs you to check out Ford’s other vehicles while it’s on hiatus.
(Source: Ford.com)
According to Ford Authority , the Escape will return as an all-electric crossover SUV based on the UEV platform.
Update 10/29/2026: A Ford spokesperson told Electrek that the Ford Authority report is pure speculation and the company has not announced the Escape will return as an EV or that it will be based on the UEV platform.
If it does come to life, the Ford Escape EV would likely remain close in size to the outgoing gas model, which measures 180.1″ long, 74.1″ wide (without mirrors), and 66.1″ tall, with a 106.7″ wheelbase. That’s about the size of other compact SUVs like the Toyota RAV4 and Hyundai Tucson.
Covered Ford Fathom prototype at the Louisville Assembly Plant (Source: Ford)
The report claimed the electric Escape is expected to enter production at Ford’s Louisville Assembly Plant in 2029, possibly making it the second vehicle based on its UEV platform, following the Fathom pickup.
CEO Jim Farley confirmed on Ford’s Q3 earnings call on Wednesday that the Fathom launch “remains on track for the fourth quarter of next year.”
The Fathom is “a breakthrough product,” Farley said, adding the pickup is highly capable, innovative, and affordable.
Ford Fathom EV pickup prototype (Source: Jim Farley)
Ford will open preorders for the Fathom in early 2027, starting at $28,350 for the standard-range version. With the $1,595 delivery fee, Ford’s electric pickup will still start under $30,000, which the company says will be “right in the heart of the market.”
The Fathom will be the first vehicle to integrate Apple Maps into its navigation system. It will also be BlueCruise-capable for hands-free driving. Other standard features include Apple CarPlay and Android Auto, plus bidirectional charging capabilities.
CEO Jim Farley presents the Ford Universal EV Platform in Kentucky (Source: Ford)
Ford claims the electric pickup will offer more interior space than a Toyota RAV4, not including the added bed and frunk (front trunk).

Inside, the Fathom has a “large touchscreen display” with an easy-to-use navigation system using Apple Maps.
Ford has yet to reveal battery specs or range, but the UEV platform uses lithium iron phosphate (LFP) batteries to reduce costs. We also know the Fathom will have an NACS charge port after a few prototypes were spotted charging at a Tesla Supercharger a few months ago.
The UEV platform is flexible enough to underpin vehicles ranging from compact crossovers to pickup trucks and vans, so an electric Escape would make sense.
With the Fathom set to launch next year, we should learn more about the potential Ford Escape EV soon. Check back for updates.

Gen. Ronald P. Clark Commanding General United States Army Pacific (USARPAC), delivers a presentation on "Land Forces: The Foundation of Pacific Stability" during the first day of the annual Maneuver Warfighter Conference Sept. 15, 2026, in Marshall Auditorium at Fort Benning, Georgia. (U.S. Army photo by Daniel Marble)
WASHINGTON — The head of US Army Pacific says his command is still preparing for the potential Chinese invasion of Taiwan that US officials have warned could occur as early as next year.
“The question is, is the window still valid? The answer for us at USARPAC is yes,” Gen. Ronald Clark said Tuesday at AFCEA’s TechNet Indo-Pacific conference in Hawaii.
Known as the “Davidson window,” the timeline is named for retired Adm. Phil Davidson, former head of US Indo-Pacific Command. In 2021, Davidson told the Senate Armed Services Committee that China could develop the capability to invade Taiwan within the following six years.
The 2027 date has since served as a planning benchmark for US and allied forces preparing to deter potential Chinese aggression against the self-governed island, which Beijing claims as its territory.
Clark, who served as Davidson’s chief of staff when he made the proclamation, said Army Pacific is working to move forces and equipment in the region to deter conflict during that period.
“We’ve embarked upon a strategic approach to setting the theater that we refer to as Army Ready Forward,” Clark said. The effort involves positioning equipment, materiel and personnel on a rotational basis across the first and second island chains west of the international date line.
The goal is to be ready by April 2, 2027, he said.
“Again, it’s not a date that we think that conflict will happen. It is a period of time for which we’re snapping the chalk line to say we need to be ready by this date,” Clark added. “But we’ll continue to prepare, we’ll continue to modernize, we’ll continue to posture ourselves for the business of deterring war well beyond [2027].”
Asked about what operational challenges industry could help address over the next six months, Clark pointed to the need for both advanced capabilities and affordable systems that can be produced at scale.
The military has largely relied on bespoke and tailored equipment in recent decades, but developing and procuring such systems can be expensive and cause significant delays in getting gear to the front lines.
As a result, the Defense Department has begun emphasizing a commercial-first approach, trying to adopt good enough solutions that soldiers can immediately use during operations. That approach also calls for fielding capabilities at scale, including large numbers of low-cost drones that can overwhelm an adversary.
“We need the right balance between exquisite, high-end systems and affordable, mass-producible alternatives. Meeting that requirement demands that the industrial base adapt to provide the surge capability and capacity required in crisis,” Clark said. “Our operational requirement is clear: we must develop resilient, affordable and scalable ways to sustain forces at the tactical edge when traditional infrastructure is disrupted or unavailable. This requirement underscores an urgent need for industry partnership.”

Same A-Class Motorhome, Different Clothes: The 2027 Pilote G740FGJ Evidence Goes for Bold
8 photos
Photo: Pilote
You can't put lipstick on a pig, but you CAN take a product that's already appreciated for its features, comfort, and style and turn it into something even better by giving it a new set of "clothes." That's what Pilote is doing with the Galaxy A-Class motorhome series for 2027.
Like many other European RV specialists, Pilote is also going for an upgraded style for the 2027 model year, but the difference is that, in their case, the upgrade is more than aesthetic and actually results in more interior volume. With any RV, but particularly with the more compact ones, any increase in interior volume means more comfort and more functionality, so it's a win for the end customer.
Of the series of motorhomes produced by the French Pilote, the Galaxy is the higher-end offer in their catalog. The Galaxy series is the series of high-end integrated A-Class motorhomes, offered in two configurations, Expression and Evidence, one being the basic version and the other the "all-inclusive" equivalent.
Today, we're looking at the Pilote G740FGJ in the Evidence spec. Of the 17 floorplans available in the entire Galaxy series for 2027, this one is among the largest and most luxurious, so it's a perfect example of what Pilote understands by luxury RV-ing in a still relatively compact form factor.
Photo: Pilote Unlike what you will find in other territories (U.S., here's looking at you!), that means a yacht-like, very elegant interior, double floor construction with plenty of storage options, two separate sleeping spaces with some spatial and physical separation for privacy, and the basics in terms of creature comforts. It also means a relative compact form factor but with an interior design that does away with the feeling of being crammed in like sardines.
This floorplan debuted in 2021, but you would probably not recognize an older model as the same one that Pilote brought out at several trade shows in the fall of 2026, to present changes for the 2027 model year. The 2027 G740FGJ debuts with a brand-new face, a brand new rear, a completely redesigned interior, and the most important part, more body length.
It's not just nicer to look at , if your idea of "nice" is a square, aggressive, and arguably futuristic front end, but longer by almost 10 cm (4 inches). The 2027 model is on a Fiat CCS chassis offered standard with a 2.2-liter engine with 180 hp and an automatic transmission, and it comes in at 7.56 meters (24.8 feet) of total length.
Photo: Pilote That Fiat chassis is the 4.5-ton one, so you're looking at a maximum permissible weight of 4,250 kg (9,369 lbs) with 1,054 kg (2,323 lbs) of payload. It could still be called "lightweight" if you compare it to much larger RVs, but it can't be operated on a standard B Category driving license.
This is a 4-bed motorhome, with 4 belted seats and 5 or 6 seats around the dining table. The layout remains essentially unchanged from previous years, and it's definitely not anything you haven't seen before if you're familiar with European or Euro-style motorhomes , but the interior overhaul adds an extra note of sophistication to it. It's not super-fancy or pretentious in an annoying way, so truly elegant.
You have a front lounge slash dining area at the front, with two large face-to-face benches and the swivel captain chairs. Over the dinette is the first sleeping area, in the form of a drop-down bed that tucks discreetly, though not invisibly, into the ceiling over the cab area.
Photo: Pilote The kitchen is next, with a new large hybrid compression fridge on the campside (also a novelty for 2027) and a compact galley that feels more elevated than it needs to be. That's not a bad thing; when you have little space to work with, it helps that it looks good.
The galley comes standard with a two-burner gas cooktop and a separate sink under a glass cover, and dedicated storage under and above the counter. Accent lighting, an accent wall, and a new blacksplash that matches the black hardware help elevate this (compact) space.
The second sleeping area is at the rear, in the form of twin beds you can join into a full king by using the slatted extension and the inserts provided. These beds have overhead storage and large wardrobes underneath; they also sit on top of the huge pass-through garage that offers 116 cm (45.6 inches) of headroom, so it's perfect for hauling bigger, bulkier, and taller items.
Photo: Pilote That same garage comes fully stocked, at least by European standards. That means you get shelves and cubbies, lights, an outdoor shower, and a pair of rails to which you can secure your bikes or even one of those larger sitting scooters. Non-slip flooring is included as well.
The bathroom inside is a pass-through one, with a large shower on one side and the washroom across from it. You can use each space separately or join them into a single room, with space left to change clothes. Alternatively, you can close off the bathroom to have privacy in the bedroom.
The 2027 Pilote G740FGJ comes with the full Evidence package (black awning, rearview camera, electric step), a 6,000W Truma Combi D6E space heater and water heater, a 200Ah lithium battery and a 210W monocrystalline solar panel, a smaller gas bottle, a TV mount in the living room, and 130 liters (34 gallons) for freshwater and 95 liters (25 gallons) for gray. The wastewater tank is heated.
Photo: Pilote Pilote calls the Pilote G740FGJ in the Evidence configuration "comfort without compromise," now with an instantly recognizable exterior design. This kind of no-compromise RV life will cost you upwards of €97,790 ($109,200 at the current exchange rate), which is the starting price for the 2027 model before options.

Canadian 1971 Corvette 454 Rocks Holy Grail LS6 and Automatic Combo, It's Rarer Than Dragon Eggs
51 photos
Photo: Mecum
When the 1970 model year rolled around, America's premier sports car suffered an unexpected humiliation inside its own showroom. The Chevrolet Corvette failed to claim the top-dog spot in the division's performance roster, surrendering the horsepower crown to the mid-size Chevelle SS 454 LS6 and its 450-hp rating. That internal upset happened because the Bowtie brand abruptly retired the planned 454-cubic-inch LS7 V8 and its 460-hp output from the catalog.
Chevrolet rectified that hierarchy imbalance in 1971 by finally dropping the legendary LS6 big-block motor between the front fenders of the Stingray. However, tightening federal emissions standards and the corporate mandate for engines to run on 91-octane low-lead fuel forced engineers to lower the compression ratio to 9.0:1. It was quite the drop, from the 11.25 squeeze of 1970, and yet it still punched hard.
Consequently, the 454-cubic-inch powerplant arrived slightly detuned to 425 gross hp (325 net hp), while still generating 475 lb-ft of gross torque (down from 500).
Equipped with lightweight aluminum cylinder heads, solid lifters, forged aluminum pistons, and an 850-cfm Holley four-barrel carburetor, the LS6 remained an absolute monster – in more than one way. The ugly side of having access to pavement-wrinkling cubic inches of performance was quantified in rectangular paper portraits of dead American presidents. Or, in certain cases, legal tender snapshots of the queen. Queen of England. More on that in a minute.
Photo: Mecum Detroit priced the LS6 at $1,221. A lot of money, considering the base Corvette started at $5,496 (coupe), or $5,259 (ragtop). The perfect explanation for scarcity, and the perfect reason to rejoyce when seeing one in the flesh.
One pristine example of this brief big-block era is the car in the gallery, chassis 194371S118779, a Classic White coupe that was sold new in Canada, and spent its first 52 years in the Great White North, in Quebec, Canada.
According to General Motors of Canada and Vintage Vehicle Services documentation, the coupe rolled off the St. Louis, Missouri assembly line on June 7, 1971. It shipped the following day to J.P. Charbonneau Autos Ltee in Montreal. It was 1 of 823 examples of its model number imported for sale in Canada that year, carrying a total factory sticker price of $8,760.80, including $2,132.35 in options. That’s CANADIAN dollars, hence the queen reference from earlier.
Photo: Mecum The car remained in its home province for decades and was acquired in 1994 by a caretaker from Trois-Rivières, Quebec, who kept it for 28 years. Beginning in 2018, that long-term owner commissioned a comprehensive four-year refurbishment to return the aging big-block coupe to showroom glory. The bodywork received a fresh coat of code-972 Classic White paint, while the cabin retained its code-412 Dark Blue vinyl bucket seats and trim.
In January 2023, the Canadian owner parted ways with the freshly refurbished Stingray on Bring a Trailer, where it sold for $135,000 with approximately 36,874 miles showing on its odometer. The winning bidder brought the Corvette back to the United States, where it was briefly marketed by Paramount Classic Cars in Hickory, North Carolina.
It subsequently entered the care of another enthusiast who pursued top-tier historical validation and judging. In January of this year, it crossed the Mecum auction block at the Kissimmee event. It hammered for $102,500.
Photo: Mecum Those efforts paid off handsomely during the 2026 judging season. In May 2026, the coupe earned a National Corvette Restorers Society Top Flight Award at the Wisconsin Chapter meet, achieving a remarkable net score of 95.7 out of 100. Less than a month later, on June 13, 2026, the National Corvette Certification Board awarded the white big-block its coveted Bloomington Gold Certification, confirming its exceptional preservation and factory-correct mechanical execution.
What makes this Canadian-delivered coupe so desirable is the extreme scarcity of its drivetrain. The LS6 engine was a one-year-only option for the Corvette, offered exclusively during the 1971 model year before vanishing forever. Out of 21,801 total Corvettes manufactured that year, buyers ordered just 188 examples with the $1,221 LS6 engine option.
That tiny figure makes the 1971 LS6 rarer than the famous L88 big-block across its multi-year run. To be fair, there was a distinct batch of a dozen units equipped with the same 454-cube LS6, sold under the ZR2 “Special Purpose Engine Package.” It doesn’t take the IQ of a quantum physicist to determine what that purpose was, but the price of admission was matching: $1,747. So, a grand total of 176 “normal” LS6 Vettes were made and sold during the 1971 model year.
Photo: Mecum Breaking down those cheaper LS6s by body style reveals that the vast majority mirrored this Classic White example. While total 1971 production saw 14,680 T-top coupes outnumber 7,121 convertibles by more than 2 to 1, the LS6 split was similarly skewed. Historians and registry experts account for 138 coupes and only 50 convertibles equipped with the 425-hp V8, making either body style a prized catch for serious American muscle collectors.
The transmission breakdown adds another layer of intrigue to the 1971 LS6 story. The ZR2 Special Purpose LS6 Engine Package, which mandated the heavy-duty M22 Rock Crusher 4-speed manual gearbox. Because Chevrolet produced 130 total M22 transmissions in 1971—with 8 going to small-block ZR1s—110 regular LS6 Corvettes received the M22.
The remaining 66 cars without the heavy-duty M22 were split almost evenly between the no-cost M21 close-ratio 4-speed manual and the M40 3-speed Turbo Hydra-Matic 400 automatic. Notably, 1971 marked the first time Chevrolet allowed buyers to pair a solid-lifter big-block engine with an automatic gearbox.
Photo: Mecum Of the roughly 33 automatic LS6 Corvettes built, only 7 were convertibles, leaving around 26 automatic coupes like this Montreal-delivered time capsule. Holy Grail? It’s safe to say it can snuggly fit that bill. Speaking of bills, the window sticker presents a short, but fat list of options:
Equipped with that rare M40 automatic transmission, a 3.36:1 Positraction rear axle, J50 vacuum power brakes, N40 hydraulic power steering, A31 power windows, and a U79 AM/FM stereo with a 4-speaker system, this Stingray cost $8,760.80 CAD when new, of which $2,132.35 were the add-ons (the engine alone cost $1,365.85).
Usually, cars like this go for $150k USD or more at auctions, making this particular white example an anomaly. The odometer reads 36,904 miles (so it covered 30 miles in the last 46 months), and I only have one more question about it: what’s the high bid going to be at the Mecum Kansas City auction on December 5? If you have any thoughts, drop them in the comments.

JACKSONVILLE, Fla. — Rising diesel fuel prices are putting increasing financial pressure on Florida trucking companies, with fuel costs surpassing driver compensation as the largest operating expense for some fleets.
Florida Trucking Association CEO Scott Perry said the combination of higher diesel prices , insurance premiums, equipment costs and driver wages is squeezing motor carriers already struggling with tighter margins.
“Traditionally, driver pay was the number one line item on the P&L,” Perry told FreightWaves during an interview at the WEX OTR Summit in Jacksonville, Florida. “Fuel has surpassed that in many instances, and it’s extremely challenging for them to absorb that if they don’t have good fuel charge mechanisms or recapture ability with their customers.”
Perry, a trucking industry veteran with more than 35 years of experience, said carriers without adequate fuel surcharge arrangements are particularly vulnerable to sudden price increases.
He cited a roughly 70% year-over-year increase in fuel costs, warning that such a surge could be catastrophic for carriers unable to recover the additional expense from customers.
While he said he was unaware of any Florida Trucking Association members that had closed or laid off workers specifically because of the recent fuel increases, he acknowledged that financial pressures are mounting.
“I’ve had several that it’s definitely compressing their ability to operate with increases in insurance that they’ve been absorbing over the last three, four, five years or more, the pressure on wages from a driver retention standpoint,” Perry said.
“All of that combined adds up to generally a negative margin business that can’t be sustained forever.”
Perry said Florida trucking companies are becoming somewhat more optimistic about freight rates heading into 2027 as trucking capacity continues to tighten.
However, he cautioned that much of the improvement is being driven by fewer available trucks rather than a significant increase in freight demand.
“I think there is some improved confidence with rates and what they’re seeing in rate structures right now,” Perry said. “As we’ve heard and read, there’s not a real demand increase in many instances. It’s capacity is being taken out of the market.”
Perry said higher freight rates could help carriers recover some of their operating expenses, but much of the additional revenue is currently being absorbed by rising diesel costs.
He also said some shippers have attempted to reverse the substantial rate increases granted during the COVID-19 pandemic, despite trucking companies facing significantly higher operating expenses than they did before 2020.
“We’ve seen insurance costs go up substantially. Diesel rates are up substantially. Labor rates are up substantially,” Perry said. “Those don’t align with the depressing rates back to pre-COVID era. It just doesn’t.”
Perry said trucking companies need sustainable rates to maintain profitability and continue investing in their fleets.
He warned that many carriers are delaying equipment replacement because of financial pressures, potentially creating additional challenges involving reliability, productivity and driver retention.
“There’s got to be realism in the rates,” Perry said. “There’s got to be recognition that those costs are real. There has to be the ability for those carriers to make a profit so that they can reinvest in their businesses.”
Florida expands truck parking along I-4 corridor
Beyond operating costs, Perry said Florida is making progress on one of the trucking industry’s longstanding infrastructure challenges: the shortage of safe truck parking .
He said the state began 2026 with approximately 2,100 public-access truck parking spaces and is moving forward with a four-phase project to add another 922 spaces.
A groundbreaking ceremony for the project took place in July.
Most of the additional parking spaces are planned along the Interstate 4 corridor, which connects the Tampa and Orlando regions and carries significant commercial truck traffic.
“That will absolutely help put a dent in the need for secure parking, easily accessible parking,” Perry said.
However, he emphasized that the additional spaces would not eliminate Florida’s truck parking shortage.
“Will 3,000 public access parking spaces serve the entire need for the industry? No, it won’t,” Perry said. “Is this a significant step in the right direction? It absolutely is.”
Perry said the shortage can force drivers to choose between complying with federal hours-of-service regulations and stopping in potentially unsafe locations, including highway shoulders and exit ramps.
He said that expanding truck parking is essential to both driver safety and fleet productivity.
“We need to provide them with solutions that give them access to maximize their productivity for their driving hours, have a safe place to park and get their rest break,” Perry said.
Florida carriers support stronger enforcement
Perry also expressed support for federal efforts to strengthen trucking safety enforcement, including increased scrutiny of non-domiciled commercial driver’s licenses, English-language proficiency requirements and electronic logging device compliance.
Florida trucking companies generally support efforts to identify carriers that circumvent federal regulations and gain an unfair competitive advantage over compliant fleets, he said.
Perry specifically praised Federal Motor Carrier Safety Administration Administrator Derek Barrs, who previously served with the Florida Highway Patrol.
“They appreciate the fact that he’s pushing to eliminate those carriers who are breaking the rules, bending the rules, manipulating the rules,” Perry said.
He also supports proposed safeguards aimed at preventing the manipulation of electronic logging devices, which are used to track drivers’ hours of service .
Tampering with ELD records can allow drivers to operate beyond legally permitted hours, creating risks for truck drivers and the traveling public.
“Anything we can do to make sure that drivers aren’t operating beyond the legally allowable hours and there’s no manipulation of ELDs to extend those hours and create unsafe circumstances … can only improve public safety,” Perry said.
He said the association supports enforcement measures that promote a level playing field among motor carriers while improving highway safety.
Carriers need sustainable margins heading into 2027
Perry said trucking companies remain hopeful that improving freight rates will eventually provide some relief from years of weak margins.
However, he warned that a meaningful recovery must allow carriers to cover operating expenses and invest in replacement equipment.
New trucks, insurance and labor have become substantially more expensive, he said, making it increasingly difficult for carriers to operate profitably at freight rates comparable to those before the pandemic.
Delaying equipment investments can create additional problems for fleets already struggling to retain qualified drivers and maintain productivity.
“If they’re not able to reinvest in their business, they’re just buying time and postponing the inevitable,” he said.

Photo: 19Bozzy92/YouTube
There's no denying that Porsche has built some of the greatest race cars out there. Likewise, there's no denying that the Germans have a very long list of successful motorsport rigs. It all started with the 356 and 550 Spyder in the 1950s and still goes on with the 963 and 911.
Porsche has dominated various racing series over the years, but it's been particularly successful on the endurance scene. The Germans have the most wins at the 24 Hours of Le Mans, 19, with the next automaker boasting only 13 victories. These wins were achieved between 1970 and 2017.
No fewer than eight Porsches took the checkered flag first at Circuit de la Sarthe. The 919 Hybrid won in the 2010s, while the 911 GT1 and WSC-95 scored wins in the 1990s. The 1980s were literally dominated by the 956 and 962, while the 936 and 935 won the event in the second half of the 1970s.
But I'm here to talk about Porsche's first Le Mans winner, the 917 . And that's mainly because I also want to show you footage of the 917K that was spotted at a vintage racing event at Imola. It's also wearing the iconic Gulf livery.
The 917 was born in the late 1960s, following a regulation change that limited Group 6 engine displacement to 3.0 liters. At the same time, the Commission Sportive Internationale allowed Group 4 sports cars to complete using engines of up to 5.0 liters. However, these cars had to be street-legal and produced in at least 50 units (later dropped to 25).
Unable to defeat the Ford GT40 with a 907 racer powered by a 3.0-liter flat-eight in 1968, Porsche set out to create a Group 4 racer. With only a few months to spare until the start of the 1969 season, Porsche tasked the legendary Hans Mezger with building a new flat-12 powerplant. The resulting 4.5-liter mill delivered around 550 horsepower.
Porsche then built a brand-new car around that engine. And it managed to produce 25 units in just ten months, in time for the homologation deadline. Lightweight and aerodynamic, the 917 was capable of speeds in excess of 200 mph (322 kph). However, both cars that entered the 1969 24 Hours of Le Mans failed to finish.
Next year, Porsche returned with a revised, short-tail version of the racer. The 917K debuted at Circuit de la Sarthe, won the race, and then went on to win six of the remaining nine events of the endurance championship. A revised version won Porsche's second Le Mans in 1971.
Although the 917K was retired after the 1971 season, Porsche continued to race other iterations of the car through 1973. The Can-Am-spec 917/30 is perhaps the most radical race car ever created thanks to a twin-turbocharged engine good for up to 1,500 horsepower.
The car you see here did not win at Le Mans, but it's an authentic 917K and sports one of the most iconic liveries out there: the blue-and-orange of Gulf Oil . The vehicle appears to be chassis 014, which made its debut at the 24 Hours of Daytona. Driven by Jo Siffert and Brian Redman, the Porsche finished in second place. The car was also raced at Spa and Watkins Glen that year.
The car belongs to a Japanese collector now, and I bet it spends most of its time in storage. Fortunately, the owner agreed to have his 917K paraded at Imola so we can hear its vintage flat-12 powerplant scream. Yup, it's one of those videos you need to watch with the volume cranked up.

source_document.body:
Curtiss-Wright Corp. will invest $30 million to expand its manufacturing facility in Round Rock, Texas, to increase production capacity for pressure and temperature sensors used in commercial nuclear reactors and industrial applications. The investment is part of the company’s broader effort to expand its nuclear supply chain capabilities as existing reactors undergo modernization and new nuclear projects advance toward construction.
The Davidson, North Carolina-based company announced the expansion Oct. 29 , saying the project would support its Naval & Power segment by increasing manufacturing capacity for pressure and temperature sensors and providing space for additional instrumentation and control (I&C) technologies, including radiation monitoring systems.
The project will enlarge the facility’s manufacturing footprint, improve production flow, and create additional space for an Advanced Innovation Center (AIC), a metrology testing laboratory, and a project management office. Curtiss-Wright also expects to increase employment at the site, although it did not disclose the planned floor-space addition, production capacity increase, construction schedule, or number of new positions.
“This expansion and investment in our Round Rock operations positions Curtiss-Wright to meet growing customer demand for our critical temperature and pressure sensors supporting the safe and reliable operation of existing and new-build commercial nuclear reactors,” said Lynn M. Bamford, chair and CEO of Curtiss-Wright. “As investments in reliable energy infrastructure and advanced nuclear technologies continue to create opportunities across the supply chain, Curtiss-Wright is prepared to support our customers with the manufacturing capacity, technical capabilities, and product portfolio to effectively meet anticipated market growth.”
Pressure and temperature instrumentation is essential to nuclear plant operation, providing measurements used to monitor process conditions, support reactor control, and detect abnormal operating conditions. Radiation monitoring systems similarly support radiological surveillance and plant safety. The proposed metrology laboratory would strengthen the site’s measurement and testing capabilities, while the AIC would provide engineering space for product development.
The Round Rock investment follows a larger manufacturing expansion Curtiss-Wright disclosed in July at its Cheswick, Pennsylvania, facility. That $80 million project is intended to support increased production for U.S. Navy programs and commercial nuclear applications, including future Westinghouse AP1000 and small modular reactor (SMR) projects.
During a Sept. 15 Morgan Stanley investor conference, Chief Financial Officer Christopher Farkas said the Cheswick investment would create approximately 150 jobs over three years. Funding would come from Curtiss-Wright, the Navy’s Maritime Industrial Base initiative, and Pennsylvania state support.
Farkas said Curtiss-Wright’s capital spending had increased approximately 30% in 2024 and 50% in 2025, and was expected to rise another 30% in 2026. He linked the spending increases to anticipated manufacturing demand and said the company expected profitable growth to support its investments while continuing to generate additional free cash flow.
Advanced Nuclear Projects Expand Equipment Opportunities
Curtiss-Wright’s nuclear business supplies equipment and services to operating reactors, plant life-extension projects, reactor restarts, and new-build facilities. Its portfolio includes reactor coolant pumps, valves, I&C systems, and other specialized equipment used in nuclear applications.
The company’s second-quarter Form 10-Q reported that Naval & Power segment revenue increased 7% year over year to approximately $410 million during the quarter ended June 30. Growth included an additional $10 million in its power and process business, primarily from commercial nuclear products supporting next-generation reactors and higher government nuclear sales. For the first six months of 2026, Naval & Power revenue reached approximately $813 million, up 13% from the comparable period of 2025.
During the September conference, CEO Bamford and Farkas outlined how Curtiss-Wright is positioning its manufacturing operations to capture nuclear equipment demand across several markets. Bamford said its reactor coolant pump technology originated in U.S. naval nuclear propulsion programs before being adapted for commercial nuclear plants and subsea pumping applications. The company has similarly developed valve technologies that can serve industrial process and nuclear markets.
That crossover supports a strategy of extending established engineering capabilities into additional applications, company executives suggested. Bamford acknowledged that naval business carries some of the lower return-on-sales margins within the Naval & Power segment, although she characterized it as strongly cash-flow positive. Curtiss-Wright did not provide a separate commercial nuclear profit margin.
The company is also pursuing additional naval manufacturing work through government-supported industrial base investments. Bamford said Curtiss-Wright’s cumulative Maritime Industrial Base funding had increased from approximately $15 million at its 2024 investor day to nearly $100 million by September 2026. The funding supports increased production, repair capacity, and potential second-source manufacturing work for existing naval platforms.
For commercial nuclear, Curtiss-Wright has been preparing for prospective reactor coolant pump orders associated with Westinghouse’s AP1000 program. Bamford said the company remained engaged with Westinghouse multiple times a week, sometimes daily, and had undertaken extensive capacity planning, commercial negotiations, and supplier preparations.
Curtiss-Wright had been working with its supply chain for approximately two years to prepare for the anticipated orders. During the September conference, Bamford said the company still expected an initial AP1000 pump order in 2026, although the timing depended on Westinghouse securing a corresponding reactor order from a utility or an international project, potentially in Poland.
The potential equipment value extends beyond reactor coolant pumps. Bamford estimated that Curtiss-Wright’s equipment content on an AP1000 could exceed $150 million once additional plant equipment selected by Westinghouse is included. She suggested equipment content for Westinghouse’s proposed AP300 SMR could be approximately half that amount.
Curtiss-Wright, notably, is also building relationships across six major SMR technology providers, targeting potential equipment content ranging from $20 million to $120 million depending on the reactor design and equipment requirements. Bamford identified X-energy and Rolls-Royce SMR as particularly substantial opportunities, with projected content toward the upper end of that range.
The company has worked on equipment design with X-energy since approximately 2020 or 2021 and has advanced into prototyping, Bamford said. That work supports development of X-energy’s Xe-100 reactor technology, including the first planned deployment at Dow’s industrial complex in Texas. Curtiss-Wright expects prototype testing to support the transition toward commercial manufacturing.
Bamford also identified significant potential equipment opportunities with Rolls-Royce SMR as the developer advances projects in Europe. She placed prospective equipment content for TerraPower and NuScale Power closer to the middle of Curtiss-Wright’s target range, while suggesting lower potential content for GE Vernova Hitachi Nuclear Energy.
The company nevertheless remains selective about capital deployment. During the September conference, Farkas said acquisitions must support Curtiss-Wright’s long-term financial objectives, including its 19% return-on-sales target, revenue growth, cash generation, and return on invested capital. Bamford said the company had declined potential acquisitions carrying excessive valuations, even as commercial nuclear remained among its areas of interest.
The Round Rock expansion adds manufacturing capacity for instrumentation used across operating and future nuclear facilities, complementing Curtiss-Wright’s larger equipment manufacturing investments in Pennsylvania. However, the company has not identified specific reactor programs or customer orders tied directly to the Texas investment.

source_document.body:
VIENNA — Canada and the European Union plan to deepen cooperation on satellite services, Arctic maritime capabilities and critical materials for defense industries at a two-day summit in Montreal that began on Thursday, according to a draft joint statement.
The proposed measures would advance a broader strategic partnership that calls for Canada and Europe to assume greater responsibility for shared security while reinforcing NATO. The draft , first reported by Politico, does not announce new troop deployments or weapons purchases.
Under the current wording, Canada is promised negotiations for access to services from Europe’s Galileo satellite constellation, as well as exploring Canadian participation in the European IRIS² satellite communications project.
Canada’s vast natural resources appear to be of particular interest to Brussels, with an entire section dedicated to energy and critical raw materials. The draft proposes exploring stockpiling of critical resources needed by civilian and defense industries to cushion supply chains against market fluctuations and geopolitical disruption.
There’s already some dissonance about some specific wording. In mid-September, European Commission President Ursula von der Leyen announced her plan to make Canada the EU’s first “associate member” – to the surprise of some European capitals. Now, the draft joint document for the ongoing summit has removed this language, speaking instead of an “ever-closer association of Canada to the EU, short of full membership itself.”
Canada is choosing not to get caught up in the war of terminology, with Politico quoting Carney as saying that “the good news is it doesn’t matter about specific names or nomenclature.”
Two key unifiers have driven Europe and Canada closer together: Russia’s war against Ukraine, and U.S. President Donald Trump. Canada launched Operation Reassurance in 2014 following Russia’s invasion of Ukraine and has led NATO’s multinational battle group in Latvia since 2017. Cooperation and coordination deepened further after Russia’s full-scale invasion of Ukraine in 2022.
Trump’s threats against NATO, Europe and Canadian sovereignty alike have accelerated the integration process. Particularly the Arctic has emerged as an area of interest. In February, Canada and Denmark signed a memorandum on defense cooperation amid Trump’s insistence that Greenland become a part of the United States, having threatened military force. Pointedly, the agreement with Ottawa was signed with Danish, Greenlandic and Faroese delegates present. It covered innovation, industrial cooperation, mutual logistics support, personnel, training and exercises.
And in March, Canada, Denmark, Finland, Iceland, Norway and Sweden held a summit in Oslo that laid the cornerstone for an Arctic-centric, security-focused format and concrete actions to secure an area that these countries increasingly perceive as a zone of joint security interests, especially vis-à-vis Russia and, to a lesser extent, China.
Finland and Norway also separately signed Arctic security-themed agreements with Canada in April and March, respectively, covering intelligence sharing, interoperability, logistics and maritime topics like the building of icebreakers, among other topics.
In July, Canada announced its intention to buy up to twelve new German-Norwegian submarines, preferring the European boats over a South Korean offer, just a few weeks after Ottawa singled out Sweden’s Saab as the preferred candidate to supply it with six new airborne early warning and control aircraft.
Around the same time, Canada secured preferential access to procurement under the EU’s Security Action for Europe (SAFE) defense-financing program, allowing Canadian-origin components to account for up to 80% of the procurement value of equipment purchased with its loans.

U.S. Marines with Marine Attack Squadron (VMA) 223 prepare AIM-120 AMRAAM missiles for loading onto an AV-8B Harrier II at Marine Corps Air Station Cherry Point, North Carolina, Aug. 5, 2025. (U.S. Marine Corps photo by Lance Cpl. Bryan Giraldo)
WASHINGTON — The US and Japan have finalized a plan to assemble the Advanced Medium-Range Air-to-Air Missile (AMRAAM) in Japan amid a crunch for munitions, according to Japanese Defense Minister Shinjiro Koizumi.
In remarks posted by the Japanese Defense Ministry, Koizumi confirmed the AMRAAM agreement covers “the establishment of a final assembly and inspection facility in Japan,” according to a Google translation. The weapon is “essential” for F-35 Joint Strike Fighters , Koizumi said, which are operated by Washington and Tokyo among other international partners.
“This is a groundbreaking agreement that will not only ensure the acquisition of equipment needed by both Japan and the United States, but will also strengthen Japan’s defense industry base,” Koizumi said Wednesday during a press conference on the sidelines of the Association of Southeast Asian Nations (ASEAN) Defense Ministers’ Meeting in the Philippines.
The defense minister did not share which Japanese industry partner was picked to assemble the missile. Koizumi additionally did not include a timeline for opening the facility, or its expected output.
Manufactured by RTX subsidiary Raytheon, the AMRAAM is a key air defense weapon that can be fired by aircraft and ground-based launchers. The missile is in high demand amid conflicts in Ukraine and the Middle East, and ramping up its production is a key focus of military planners.
The AMRAAM agreement follows a September contract award to Raytheon worth up to over $20 billion under a five-year agreement, with options for an additional two years of production. That contract will “nearly” double the weapon’s production, the Pentagon said at the time — as long as US lawmakers provide the necessary funding.
Koizumi additionally disclosed that the US and Japan “agreed to share the necessary technical information to achieve increased production” of the Standard Missile-3 Block IIA, a primarily ship-based interceptor used to bat down ballistic missiles. The SM-3 Block IIA is a joint program between the US and Japan, though Koizumi did not share how much the agreement may raise the interceptor’s production rate.
A Tuesday readout of a meeting between Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth published by the Pentagon does not discuss the AMRAAM or SM-3 agreements. However it says Hegseth “welcomed Japan’s efforts to strengthen its defense industrial capacity, and both leaders committed to continue close coordination on critical munitions production.”
RTX deferred to the US Defense Department when asked to comment on the agreements. A Pentagon spokesperson did not respond to an inquiry by press time.
The AMRAAM and SM-3 agreements were both part of “Operation Supercharge,” a joint US-Japan effort to boost defense technology cooperation, according to Koizumi. The two countries are deepening defense ties amid a historic ramp up in defense spending in Japan as the threat of Chinese expansion looms large over the region.
Koizumi and Hegseth “shared a sense of crisis regarding the increasingly severe regional situation and agreed to strengthen the deterrence and response capabilities of the Japan-US alliance at an even faster and stronger pace,” Koizumi said during the Wednesday press conference, without explicitly referencing China.

Hyundai is launching a new mass-market electric SUV to be made in India, expected to go on sale as the IONIQ P.
Hyundai hints at IONIQ P as new entry-level EV for India
After disguised prototypes have been spotted testing in public several times now, we may know the name of Hyundai’s compact electric SUV.
During its third-quarter earnings call, Hyundai said it would introduce the IONIQ P in India following the new Bayon.
Although it didn’t explicitly confirm the name of the upcoming model, codenamed HE1i, it’s expected to go on sale as the IONIQ P as the latest addition to Hyundai’s dedicated IONIQ EV lineup.

Mr. Tarun Garg, Managing Director & Chief Executive Officer of Hyundai Motor India, declared on Wednesday that the “Launch of Bayon marks the onset of our golden product cycle. He added We are also fully geared up for the launch of [our] dedicated mass market EV in Q4 FY27.”
The vehicle was first spotted earlier this year driving near Hyundai’s Sriperumbudur plant in Chennai, India, the “Detroit of Asia,” as it’s known.
Hyundai has yet to confirm the name, but the vehicle carried an “HE1i” tag, suggesting it was an IONIQ model.
Hyundai prototype believed to be its entry-level EV for India (Source: Autohome/ Team-BHP.com)
Previous electric test vehicles, like the IONIQ 5 and IONIQ 9, were tagged with “ME” and “NE,” with the “E” indicating they are based on the dedicated E-GMP platform.
The new entry-level EV will sit below the Creta Electric as a smaller, lower-priced electric SUV that will serve as a cornerstone of Hyundai’s growth plans in India.
During its CEO Investor Day in August, Hyundai Motor announced plans to launch 100 new or refreshed vehicles between now and 2030, including 58 in North America, 49 in South Korea, 41 in Europe, and 26 in India.
Hyundai new hybrid, EREV, and EVs launching over the next 8 months (Source: Hyundai Motor Company)
Alongside the recently launched IONIQ 3 and new Tucson, Hyundai previewed a new electric A-SUV for India, a global B-SUV, and another B-SUV for Europe.
Hyundai Motor is investing $15.5 billion to expand its presence in India by 2032, including expanding manufacturing capacity and building a local supply chain. The new entry-level EV will be Hyundai’s first produced locally in India. By 2030, Hyundai expects total production capacity to reach 1.1 million units in India.
Hyundai’s global sales fell 10% year over year in the third quarter to 931,211 units. India, meanwhile, was its fastest-growing market with sales up 9.5% in Q3 to over 150,000 units.
Will Hyundai bring the compact electric SUV to other global markets? The company said India will serve as an “important export hub,” but didn’t offer any further details.
A covered prototype was recently caught testing in South Korea by ShortsCar , initially thought to be the IONIQ 4 or possibly IONIQ 1.
Hyundai already exports vehicles made in India to global markets like the UK, Central and South America, and the Middle East, so it wouldn’t be a surprise.
In September, Hyundai’s domestic sales and exports from India rose 11% to 77,916, the highest monthly total yet.

RXO remains a publicly-traded company as it prepares to be acquired by C.H. Robinson , posting its earnings Thursday that showed mostly positive numbers in all key categories.
Given the pending deal with C.H. Robinson, RXO (NYSE: RXO) did not hold an earnings call with analysts. The summary slides that also accompany earnings were not released either.
On the growth side, the company’s revenue was $1.9 billion in the third quarter, compared to $1.4 billion a year ago. Revenue was $1.8 billion in the second quarter.
One key metric that was slightly negative was company-wide gross margin at 14.6%, compared to 16.5% a year ago. However, the third quarter performance was improved on the 13.9% margin in the second quarter.
Adjusted EBITDA numbers were improved. The $51 million recorded in the third quarter came with a 2.7% EBITDA margin, up from 2.3% a year ago when EBITDA was $32 million. The EBITDA margin in the second quarter also was 2.3%.
RXO’s EBITDA of $51 million exceeded the forecast of $35 million to $45 million issued by RXO in its second quarter earnings. “We exceeded the high end of our third-quarter profit outlook, demonstrating the momentum we’re building across RXO,” RXO CEO Drew Wilkerson said in the company’s prepared statement releasing earnings.
One of the more positive figures in the earnings was the fact that RXO made money for the second consecutive quarter. RXO had adjusted net income of 2 cents per share in the third quarter after a second quarter net income of 6 cents per share. Profitability at RXO has been spotty for several years, with some positive net income quarters reported but more frequently showing red ink.
Brokerage volume for the company–the specifics of which are not disclosed by RXO–was up 2% from a year ago. RXO also said truckload volume increased all three months of the quarter.
The mix at RXO’s truckload segment shifted heavily toward the spot market in the quarter. It accounted for 51% of volume, up from 59% a year ago and 42% sequentially.
“This helped drive the largest sequential gross profit per load growth rate in more than four years,” the company’s prepared statement said.
LTL volume was up 2% from a year ago, RXO said. The company’s Last Mile segment–which C.H. Robinson (NASDAQ: CHRW) touted as an attractive part of the RXO business that would strengthen the acquiring company–recorded a 5% increase in stops compared to a year ago.

Kodiak AI signed a binding agreement Wednesday to put its autonomous driving system in 75 trucks owned and operated by DTL Transport, a Fresno, California, carrier that runs cross-country team loads for grocers.
The deal moves Kodiak’s Driver-as-a-Service model from Permian Basin sand hauling onto interstate freight lanes, though Kodiak has yet to run a driverless truck on a public highway. Kodiak is ranked No. 12 in the 2027 FreightTech 25 list.
Under the agreement, DTL will own and operate the trucks and pay Kodiak a per-mile fee to use the Kodiak Driver. DTL, a family-run carrier that has hauled dry and refrigerated freight for more than 36 years, runs a fleet of more than 100 trucks. The release did not disclose the rate, the contract term or when the first of the 75 will run without a driver.
“This binding agreement reinforces what I have said from the beginning: The Driver-As-A-Service business model is tailor-made for commercial trucking,” said Don Burnette, Kodiak’s founder and CEO.
Lanes target hours-of-service limits
DTL will start on two lanes Kodiak has already tested: between Dallas and El Paso, Texas, and on Interstate 20 between Dallas and Atlanta. In 2023, Kodiak began hauling Forward Air freight on the Atlanta lane with teams of safety drivers aboard.
Carriers run teams to get past a solo driver’s limits under federal hours-of-service rules , which bar a property-carrying driver from driving more than 11 hours within a 14-hour window after 10 consecutive hours off duty.
Kodiak said the two routes give DTL the opportunity to operate beyond current service-hour limitations, with more lanes to be added over time. The release did not say whether the driverless trucks will replace DTL’s teams on those lanes.
“By integrating this technology into our fleet, complementing our experienced, professional workforce, we can expand capacity, enhance safety and drive innovation forward,” said Lucky Dosanjh, DTL’s president and CEO.
California pilot preceded the deal
The agreement follows a September pilot in which the Kodiak Driver hauled perishable goods for DTL 225 miles from Fresno to Los Angeles on Interstate 5 and State Route 99. A safety driver stayed behind the wheel, as required by the testing permit the California Department of Motor Vehicles granted Kodiak in August, Heavy Duty Trucking reported .
Kodiak said those were the first commercial goods autonomously hauled by a Class 8 truck in California.
Kodiak’s highway launch still ahead
Kodiak plans to launch driverless highway service by the end of this year, hauling IKEA freight on Interstate 45 between Dallas and Houston, and still has to close its long-haul safety case. Its Autonomy Readiness Measure reached 93% at the end of August , up from 84% in February.
As of June 30, Kodiak’s 35 customer-owned driverless trucks ran for Atlas Energy Solutions in the Permian Basin. Kodiak has committed to growing that fleet to 100 trucks by mid-2027.
The company reported second-quarter revenue of $3.5 million, up from $503,000 a year earlier, and a $43.7 million operating loss. It ended June with $151.1 million in cash, cash equivalents and marketable securities. Kodiak AI’s third-quarter earnings are set to release Thursday, Nov. 5 after market close.
Why it matters: Driverless trucks suit team expedite work, where freight has to keep moving past a solo driver’s hours limit. DTL can’t put that to work on its 75 trucks until Kodiak closes its long-haul safety case and launches driverless on public highways.

source_document.body:
Container freight rates climbed on major Asia-Europe and trans-Pacific routes last week despite signs of cooling demand, as congestion and canceled sailings supported prices.
Carriers’ accelerating return to the Red Sea is reshaping shipping schedules, analyst and SONAR data contributor Freightos (NASDAQ: CRGO ) said in an update, while a potential strike at Los Angeles-Long Beach adds another source of uncertainty for cargo owners.
Nearly two-thirds of capacity deployed between Asia and Europe is now routing through the Red Sea, according to Alphaliner. Its survey of the 10 largest carrier networks found that 24 of 46 direct services were using the passage, representing 63% of deployed capacity. The share was higher on Mediterranean routes, at 70%, than on North Europe services, at 58%.
Israeli carrier Zim announced a return to the Red Sea for its joint Asia-U.S. East Coast service with Mediterranean Shipping Co. The move is notable because Yemen-based Houthi rebels backing Hamas in Gaza declared the Bab el-Mandeb Strait in the southern Red Sea closed to Israel-linked vessels as recently as August.
The return remains uneven. Some services are using the Suez Canal on voyages toward Europe while continuing to sail around Africa on their return journeys, emphasizing carriers’ continued caution about the route.
Typhoon Champi brought fresh disruption to East Asia last week, closing Taiwanese container ports, including Kaohsiung, Keelung and Taipei, on Friday. The storm largely spared East China port operations before weakening as it moved toward Japan.
Major Chinese container hubs are still recovering from earlier summer storms, with many yet to return fully to normal operations. That congestion has helped support freight rates even as demand eases after the peak shipping season, according to the update.
The shift back to the shorter Red Sea route may also be complicating the recovery. Ships arriving ahead of schedules built around longer Africa voyages can bunch together at destination ports, adding pressure to terminals already working through backlogs.
Asia-Europe freight prices have risen since mid-October, supported by congestion and carriers’ efforts to restrict available capacity through blank sailings, or canceled departures. Carriers are seeking further increases in November, although forwarders have reported discounted offers and questioned whether the higher prices will hold.
The Freightos Baltic Index put last week’s Asia-North Europe rate at $3,551 per 40-foot equivalent unit, or FEU, up 3%. Prices to the Mediterranean rose 8% to $4,252 per FEU.
Carriers are pairing their November pricing plans with additional sailing cancellations. Drewry reported eight blank sailings scheduled on Asia-Europe routes for the following week, compared with two in the current week. European forwarders nevertheless said carriers had discounted their published rates during October and expected similar concessions in November.
Trans-Pacific prices also rose, defying expectations of a slowdown after China’s Golden Week holiday. Asia-U.S. West Coast rates increased 3% to $8,368 per FEU, while East Coast rates jumped 9% to $10,565, a high for the year.
Daily East Coast prices have since retreated but remained about $200 per FEU above the previous week’s level, Freightos said. The analyst noted forwarders are seeing signs that demand is cooling and space is becoming easier to secure.
At LA-Long Beach, approximately 250 port watchmen have authorized a strike that could begin Nov. 1 if contract negotiations fail.
Although the workers account for only about 2% of the ports’ International Longshore and Warehouse Union workforce, their role could give a walkout a much wider impact. The Pacific Maritime Association said terminals employing the watchmen handle roughly 85% of Long Beach’s cargo and 33% of Los Angeles’ cargo.
The employers’ association warned that other ILWU members were not expected to cross Local 26 picket lines, potentially stopping vessel, yard and gate operations at affected terminals. Negotiations remain underway, and a strike has not been confirmed.
Any work stoppage would add to existing delays affecting rail-bound containers at the port complex, according to the supplied update.
U.S. trade policy presents another approaching deadline. The White House extended its trade truce with China in late September, preserving the current arrangements on tariffs and other parts of the agreement until early January, according to the supplied update.
However, U.S. port fees on China-linked vessels remain formally scheduled top resume Nov. 10. Although much of the shipping industry expected those charges to be deferred alongside the broader truce, the U.S. Trade Representative had instead opened a request for comments on postponing them until January. That step points toward a possible delay but does not itself suspend the fees.
The update also said USTR expects to complete Section 301 investigations into excess manufacturing capacity in China and 15 other countries by year-end.
Those investigations could provide a basis for restoring tariffs to levels previously imposed under the International Emergency Economic Powers Act. Following the Supreme Court’s invalidation of IEEPA-based tariffs, replacement duties left some countries, including China, facing rates below their negotiated levels, according to the supplied account.
Even if the investigations conclude by December, the required public-comment and hearing process could push implementation of any resulting tariffs back by another couple of months, leaving a further gap between the findings and new duties.
Why it matters: Importers face uncertainty over both shipping costs and delivery times, even as the return to the Red Sea promises shorter voyages. More capacity does not automatically mean cheaper or more reliable shipping when congestion, canceled sailings and labor disputes interfere.

The Department of Energy (DOE) has closed a $5.1 billion federally guaranteed loan package for Alliant Energy’s two regulated utilities, providing access to lower-cost financing for new natural gas-fired generation, battery energy storage, liquefied natural gas (LNG) storage, and upgrades to existing power plants in Iowa and Wisconsin. The financing arrives as Alliant prepares for an increase in electricity demand of approximately 60% by 2031, driven largely by new data center customers.
DOE’s Office of Energy Dominance Financing (EDF) announced the financial close on Oct. 28, saying the investments would support more than 2.6 GW of new or upgraded power capacity. Its project summary identifies approximately 1,500 MW of new natural gas generation, 240 MW of additional capacity at existing generating units, and 1,000 MW of battery energy storage, alongside 2 billion cubic feet (Bcf) of LNG storage. Alliant’s announcement, however, lists 1.6 GW of new gas generation. Neither source identifies the specific facilities to be financed or specifies whether the electrical capacity figures represent nameplate or accredited capacity.
The package comprises two loans provided by the Federal Financing Bank (FFB) and guaranteed by DOE under Title XVII of the Energy Policy Act of 2005. According to Alliant’s Oct. 28 Form 8-K , Interstate Power and Light (IPL), its Iowa utility, can borrow up to $3.5 billion, while Wisconsin Power and Light (WPL) can borrow up to $1.626 billion. Both utilities executed their respective loan agreements on Oct. 26. Each utility is solely responsible for its borrowings, and Alliant Energy, the parent company, has no direct obligations under either agreement, the filing notes.
The close follows DOE’s Oct. 27 conditional commitment of up to $5 billion for Constellation Energy’s proposed nuclear uprates . However, unlike that financing offer, Alliant’s loan agreements have been executed, although individual advances remain subject to project-specific conditions.
“These investments will drive down energy costs for families and businesses in Iowa and Wisconsin, strengthen our nation’s electric grid, and fuel American prosperity for decades to come,” said Energy Secretary Chris Wright.
Alliant President and CEO Lisa Barton said the federal financing could lower borrowing costs as the company expands its generation portfolio. “This federally backed financing helps lower the cost of building the generation and critical energy infrastructure our customers depend on, while strengthening the grid and supporting long-term savings.”
Loan Terms Link Financing to Regulatory Approvals
Alliant projects up to $1.2 billion in cumulative customer savings over the 30-year life of the loans. EDF estimates that the financing could reduce annual interest expense by more than $46 million, subject to project qualification and financing terms. The agency also estimates the investments will support 1,630 construction jobs and 46 permanent positions.
Each advance will carry an interest rate based on the applicable U.S. Treasury rate plus 37.5 basis points, according to Alliant’s 8-K. Final maturity is May 15, 2056, and scheduled principal repayments begin in 2052 for IPL and 2053 for WPL.
The loans operate on a reimbursement basis. Each utility may request one advance per calendar quarter to recover up to 80% of eligible costs already incurred, subject to DOE environmental reviews, state regulatory approvals, and investment-grade credit ratings. Advances are available through Sept. 15, 2033, unless a facility reaches its borrowing limit or terminates earlier.
The agreements also include an early-repayment provision linked to regulatory cost recovery. If eligible project costs approved for recovery by the Iowa Utilities Commission (IUC) or Public Service Commission of Wisconsin (PSCW) fall below 95% of the applicable utility’s loan advances, the utility must repay the resulting shortfall under the agreements’ terms. The test applies two years after the advance availability period ends. Both facilities are senior unsecured, full-recourse obligations of the individual utilities.
The completed financing substantially expands Alliant’s earlier commitments. Its 2025 Form 10-K disclosed conditional commitments totaling approximately $3 billion, comprising $1.4 billion for IPL and $1.6 billion for WPL.
Alliant’s Generation Buildout Responds to Surging Data Center Demand
Alliant, headquartered in Madison, Wisconsin, serves approximately 1.01 million electric and 435,000 natural gas customers through IPL and WPL. According to its 2025 Form 10-K, IPL reported 4,274 MW of generating capacity and WPL 4,166 MW at year-end, reflecting ownership-adjusted capacity and the Midcontinent Independent System Operator’s (MISO’s) summer installed capacity conventions for conventional generation. The utilities operate natural gas, coal, wind, solar, and battery storage resources.
Large-load agreements are reshaping Alliant’s resource requirements. During the company’s July 31 earnings call , Barton said five executed electric service agreements (ESAs) were expected to increase electricity demand approximately 60% by 2031. Three major data center developments were already under construction.
So far, Google has energized transmission service in Cedar Rapids, Iowa, while QTS is advancing its seven-building campus there, targeting initial energization of 300 MW later in 2026. Meta has also begun vertical construction of its data center facilities in Beaver Dam, Wisconsin. Alliant is preparing an individual customer rate application for QTS’s proposed 900-MW project in Clinton, Iowa. It also signed a separate 370-MW Iowa data center agreement earlier in 2026 and has identified a pipeline of 2 GW to 4 GW of additional potential large-load demand.
To serve that growth, Alliant is pursuing a substantial portfolio of natural gas and energy storage projects, although it has not identified which will receive federal financing. In Iowa, IPL has begun construction activities for the 720-MW Bobcat Energy Center, a simple-cycle gas plant near its existing Marshalltown Generating Station, and a 95-MW reciprocating internal combustion engine (RICE) project in Burlington.
During the July earnings call, Chief Financial Officer Robert Durian said IPL had filed generation certificates for two other simple-cycle gas projects: the 720-MW Morgan Valley Energy Center and the 1.2-GW Riverhawk project. The utility also filed for approximately 125 MW of battery storage. Other investments include the approved 94-MW Cedar River RICE project at Prairie Creek and a 17.5-MW RICE unit at Riverside in Wisconsin.
Alliant’s 2025 annual report identifies additional approved battery storage projects at the former Lansing Generating Station (150 MW), Golden Plains (75 MW), and Whispering Willow–North (75 MW). In Wisconsin, WPL has pursued a 2-Bcf LNG storage facility in Rock County to provide additional fuel supply flexibility. Existing generating assets are also undergoing upgrades. Durian said in July that generation enhancements at Neenah and Sheboygan Falls had entered service, adding approximately 260 MW of capacity.
The utilities are also retaining existing fossil generation while developing additional resources. WPL plans to keep its ownership interests in Columbia Energy Center (596 MW) and Edgewater Unit 5 (405 MW) operating at least through 2029 while evaluating potential conversion to natural gas. Alliant maintains a voluntary target to eliminate coal from its fleet by 2040.
The investments form part of Alliant’s approximately $13.4 billion construction and acquisition program for 2026 through 2029, outlined in its 2025 Form 10-K. The plan includes approximately $5.05 billion for renewable generation and storage and $4.08 billion for gas projects, alongside distribution infrastructure investments. It also encompasses new renewable capacity, including up to 1,000 MW of proposed Iowa wind generation.
The company’s financing strategy combines operating cash flow, tax credit monetization, debt, and equity. Durian said in July that Alliant had secured approximately $1.8 billion of its identified $2.4 billion equity requirement through 2029 using forward equity agreements.
Alliant maintains that large-load customers must cover their incremental service costs while creating opportunities to stabilize rates for existing customers. IPL operates under a retail electric base-rate moratorium through September 2029, and management has suggested additional load growth could extend the period before its next general rate review.
“Look, the math is self-explanatory. By growing, we’re able to keep rates flat in Iowa,” Barton said during the July earnings call.
Alliant is scheduled to report its third-quarter earnings after market close on Oct. 29, followed by an Oct. 30 conference call that could provide further details on its capital investments, data center demand, and use of the newly completed federal financing.

All British-Built Ariel Atom and Nomad Vehicles Are Now Available in the U.S.
64 photos
Photo: Ariel
British carmaker Ariel is not exactly mainstream, but that doesn't mean it doesn't have a fair share of fans – not only in the home market, but also across the pond, in the U.S.. Whereas up until now customers there were treated to vehicles made under a licensed manufacturing program, Ariel vehicles will from now on land stateside right off the Brits’ assembly facility.
The company announced this week that, as of now, American customers get access to all four British-built models for the first time, namely the Atom 4 , Atom 4R, Arom 4RR and Nomad 2. Tasked with getting these rides into the proper hands is Arizona-based Forman Motorworks, which has been in bed with Ariel for a long time already.
We're told the first two demonstrator models designed for the American market, an Atom 4 and a 4R, are already being assembled, and they should reach the U.S. in the first quarter of next year. Customer deliveries are expected to begin in the summer of 2027.
The America-spec vehicles are already listed on Forman Motorworks' configurator , so we can form a pretty decent idea of what to expect. Spoiler alert: things are not at all different from what Ariel offers elsewhere, and the prices are quite high.
The Atom 4 in its most basic incarnation uses a Honda -sourced 2.0-liter turbocharged i-VTEC engine that's rated at 345 hp and 310 lb-ft of torque. Those are incredible numbers, if you take into account the fact that this thing weighs just 1,350 pounds (612 kg). The cost of the package: $117,000.
The Atom 4R is basically the same vehicle, but with a significant increase in power levels. That would be 395 horsepower and 369 lb-ft of torque coming from the engine, which are offered to customers for an impressive $166,500.
The third Atom in the lineup, the 4RR, not only throws in an extra consonant, but also 518 horsepower and 405 lb-ft of torque. All of that, plus an engine that revs at a maximum of 8,200 rpm, can be had for yet-to-be-specified prices, but certainly higher than when it comes to the vehicle's siblings.
We expect the sticker to read something along the lines of $280,000, and that's in part owed to the fact that this is the fastest and most powerful Atom made to date.
Finally, the Nomad 2 , the only off-road-oriented vehicle in the lineup, throws in 300 horsepower and nine inches (23 cm) of ground clearance, so that it can easily navigate rough terrain. The price sticker for this one stands at $124,400.
As a reminder, all Ariel vehicles are highly customizable, and they can also be had as rolling chassis. This basically means that every Ariel out there can take a form of its own, within a certain set of approved parts, including engines and transmissions.
